skyline.text: Why armies built for big wars lose to guerrillas
OPEC’s fifty years bought it 1.5 per cent a year
Kieślowski’s scientist father, his skating son, and a lesson in humility

footnote.text: It’s been a gamble on your part to watch it.

brief.head: Monopoly needs a state
brief.text: Cartels cannot last where anyone is free to enter a market, Amit Varma said. Lasting monopolies exist only where the state hands someone an advantage. {004-C01}

brief.head: Armies aren’t for home
brief.text: The military is built to marshal unbelievable levels of violence, Ajay Shah said. Its training, manuals and tactics are not wisely applied to India’s own people. {004-C10}

brief.head: Kyiv taken, war lost
brief.text: Even had Russia taken Kyiv, Amit Varma argued, it could never have won the counterinsurgency that followed. Ajay Shah said that had been his baseline from the start. {004-C13}

brief.head: Battleships of state
brief.text: Big Indian institutions turn slowly, Ajay Shah said, like a battleship or a super tanker. The Western way of war learns through introspection: diaries, logs and books. {004-C12}

brief.head: A book for businessmen
brief.text: Tirthankar Roy’s *A Business History of India* showed Ajay Shah how little has changed. He urged even a businessperson who has never read a book to read it. {004-R15}

thought.text: The Stone Age did not end because the world ran out of stones.
thought.who: Saudi oil minister Ahmed Zaki Yamani, quoted by Ajay Shah on how the oil age will end

lead.kicker: Ajay Shah on OPEC, Amit Varma on guerrillas and Kashmir
lead.head: Big stick, short reach
body: Ajay Shah brought a cartel that never quite ruled the oil market. Amit Varma brought armies that keep losing to guerrillas, and an argument that India keeps getting it wrong.
## Seven times in fifty years
OPEC, Shah said, was the caricature of a cartel: at its peak, all the world’s oil producers agreeing to fix a price and cut supply, and, as governments, beyond the reach of any antitrust law.
Yet crude cost about $11 a barrel in 1974 and about $77 in 2023. That is roughly seven times, he said, or about 1.5 per cent a year in real terms. {004-S01}
“You tell me that you’ve got this powerful cartel that’s controlling the price,” Shah said, “and all they’ve managed to get is about one and a half per cent real of a price hike.”
He gave three reasons. In the short run demand barely moves, because you still have to drive to work. In the long run people adjust dramatically, finding new oil, thriftier cars and substitutes.

Second, nobody likes to be extorted. If India made its call centres refuse to work for JP Morgan, Shah said, the bank would suffer for three weeks, and then the world would learn to manage without India.
“In a conflict the other guy gets a vote,” he said. {004-C03}
Third, cartels leak. Thinly populated Saudi Arabia, Kuwait and Qatar could afford to cut output, while Iran and Iraq, with large populations, kept selling.
## The buyers’ turn
Then the story ran backwards. After Russia invaded Ukraine, its crude went mainly to India and China, and the West capped the price at $60 a barrel by leaning on Western shipping and insurance firms.
Putin needed money for the war and had only two buyers left. “So suddenly, instead of OPEC being a cartel of sellers, you had China and India as a cartel of buyers,” Shah said. {004-S02}
## Winning the people
Varma’s rabbit hole began with a secondhand book in a Bangalore shop and led to David Galula’s 1960s classic on counterinsurgency.
“If a fly and a lion are fighting, the fly cannot deliver a knockout blow, and the lion cannot fly,” Varma said, borrowing Galula’s metaphor. {004-C06}
One of Mao’s generals put it as 20 per cent military and 80 per cent political. India in Kashmir, Varma argued, was more or less 100 per cent military, and alienated the people it calls its own.

If Kashmir is an integral part of India, he said, Kashmiris are Indian citizens, and the state’s job is to serve them, not rule over them. He applied Mancur Olson’s roving and stationary bandits to the Naxal areas in the same spirit.

Shah turned David Petraeus’s test, whether an operation takes more bad guys off the street than it creates, into the arithmetic of epidemics. If killing one militant creates 1.01 more on average, he said, “then you’ve had it because this thing will explode”. {004-C07}
He also warned against the securitisation of the state, in which invoking national security brings all questions to a stop.
The episode ended with books, films and a bet. Shah recommended Tirthankar Roy’s *A Business History of India*; Varma called Krzysztof Kieślowski’s *Dekalog* the pinnacle of cinematic storytelling.

Then a remark about stock indexes for vices set off Varma, a professional poker player for five years. Everything in life is a gamble, he said, watching this show included: “So well done, you’re a gambler.”

second.label: Kashmir
second.head: The year Kashmir hoped
second.deck: Amit Varma, drawing on David Devadas, on a chance India let slip
body: Kashmir had a chance in 2007, Amit Varma said. Drawing on David Devadas’s *The Generation of Rage in Kashmir*, he described a new generation sick of fighting, wanting to be programmers, engineers and artists. {004-R07}

But the security forces were entrenched, and men who had fought on the front lines in the 1990s now held senior positions. Rewards for counting heads got innocent people killed, and the need for permission for everything bred rent-seeking and extortion.

One young man refused to hand his Tata Indigo to a security man and was imprisoned. The window closed, Pakistan came in, and things went to hell. It is hard, Varma said, not to ask how you would react in a Kashmiri boy’s shoes. {004-S04}

quote.text: You’ve seen your older brother taken away by the security forces and he disappears.

second.caption: Kashmir’s lost moment of 2007

third.head: Doom forgot the price tag
body: The 1972 Club of Rome report forecast doom by mechanically extrapolating consumption, Ajay Shah said. “And what was missing in that entire thinking was the word price.” {004-C04}
Amit Varma called peak oil a crackpot conspiracy theory. {#peakoil} Scarcity raises prices, he said, and higher prices spur exploration, renewables and perhaps nuclear: “We respond to incentives.”

Shah added that lithium is not rare at all, being made in large amounts in the furnace of the stars. Serious people, he said, once drew up business plans to tow resource-rich asteroids back to Earth. {#asteroid}

Varma promptly pitched a Bollywood film: Akshay Kumar flies to an asteroid made of lithium. Shah objected that lithium is plentiful on Earth, and suggested tantalum, a name he had picked off the periodic table. {004-J04}
third.caption: the word the doomsayers forgot

p2.title: Cartels and guerrillas
p2.deck: Ajay Shah on a cartel that could not hold, Amit Varma on wars that force alone cannot win

sections.label: The sellers
sections.head: A cartoon of a cartel
sections.caption: OPEC’s fifty years of oil prices
body: OPEC, Ajay Shah said, was the caricature of a cartel. At its peak it was a coalition of all the world’s oil producers, agreeing to fix a price and to cut supply to reach it. Because its members were governments, not firms, no antitrust law could touch it.
Then he looked at the data. Crude was about $11 a barrel in 1974 and about $77 now: seven times, but only about 1.5 per cent a year in real terms. {004-S01}
## Three leaks in the pipe

The first was time. Price elasticities are low in the short term, he said: double the price and you still drive to work. But the higher price paid for exploration on a large scale, and for cars that burn less fuel. {004-C02}

The second was extortion. China tried to choke rare earths to Japan in 2012; Russia tried to choke Europe’s energy. Victims answer such hard power by cutting their exposure, and governments everywhere found ways to de-risk their economies from OPEC. {004-C03}
The third was cheating. Saudi Arabia, Kuwait and Qatar have small populations and vast oil revenues, so they could cut supply and wait. Iraq and Iran, with large populations, were keen to sell more.

~ So when Saudi Arabia pulled back one to three million barrels a day, Shah said, others made it up, from the North Sea to Russia and Mexico. The cartel’s loud promises at its meetings would not really work out once members went home.

quote.text: In the long run, however, human beings adjust dramatically.

sections.label: The buyers
sections.head: A cartel of two customers
sections.caption: the reverse OPEC
body: The most interesting period, Ajay Shah said, is the recent one. When the war in Ukraine began in February 2022, Putin’s implicit threat was that Europe would shiver in its homes through the winter. Europe called the bluff and found an array of solutions.
Russian crude went mainly to India and China instead. “India is at about 51% of Russian crude oil sales,” Shah said. {#fiftyone}

Then the West invented a new tool of economic statecraft: a cap of $60 a barrel on all Russian crude sales. {#sixty} It could be enforced because almost all the world’s shipping and shipping insurance is run out of Western countries, most notably the UK.
## Full circle

Shah doubted it would work: new tanker fleets would spring up, and the *Financial Times* reported one operating out of Bombay. But the data suggest Russian sales were choked at $60. With a war to fund and only two buyers left, Putin faced a cartel of customers who could drive a hard bargain. {004-S02}

~ The oil age itself, Shah said, may end as the Saudi oil minister Ahmed Zaki Yamani predicted, through technology, now that Europe is set on decarbonisation. {004-J09} Siberian gas may still sit in the ground a thousand years from now.

quote.text: Almost all the shipping of the world and almost all the shipping insurance of the world is run out of Western countries

sections.label: The insurgents
sections.head: Soup with a knife
sections.caption: the counterinsurgency canon
body: Amit Varma’s rabbit hole, which began with Fred Kaplan’s *The Insurgents*, led to what he called the Bible of the literature: David Galula’s *Counterinsurgency Warfare*. Galula, who had fought in China and Algeria, was once imprisoned by Mao’s men. {#galula}
His point was that fighting insurgents is very different from fighting a conventional war. Use conventional tactics, Varma said, and it is like using a fly swatter: the flies keep coming. {004-C06}
Kaplan sums up the method: push the insurgents out, hold the area, win the people’s trust, replace the insurgents’ political organisation, then mop up.
## The missing 80 per cent

One of Mao’s generals said counterinsurgency is 20 per cent military and 80 per cent political. {004-C05} T. E. Lawrence, in *Seven Pillars of Wisdom*, likened it to eating soup with a knife. India in Kashmir, Varma said, was more or less 100 per cent military.
He was not arguing against fighting terrorists from Pakistan or defending borders. But a state that claims a people as its own, he said, must serve them rather than rule them.

~ He saw the Naxal areas through Mancur Olson’s bandits. A roving bandit robs a village and leaves; a stationary bandit stays to tax it, so he builds infrastructure. {004-C08} Where the state was absent, both it and the Naxalites behaved like roving bandits.

quote.text: Will this operation take more bad guys off the street than it creates by the way it’s conducted?
quote.who: David Petraeus, as quoted by Amit Varma

sections.label: Shah’s reply
sections.head: Too important for generals
sections.caption: the securitised state
body: Ajay Shah heard in David Petraeus’s question the mathematics that COVID taught everyone. If one infected person infects more than one other, an epidemic explodes; if killing one militant creates 1.01 new ones on average, so does an insurgency. {004-C07}
He was also deeply uncomfortable with turning the military, an institution designed for overwhelming violence, on India’s own population. {004-C10}
## When fear ends the argument

Then there is what he called the securitisation of the Indian state. Once national security is invoked, all questions are supposed to stop. Emphasising fear, he said, is the surest way to wrong policies, just as harping on crises is a poor guide to financial policy. {004-C11}

The French in Algeria and the Americans in Vietnam, Iraq and Afghanistan, Shah said, changed their conduct through debate and criticism, and through intellectuals like Petraeus. India lacks that capacity, and not only in security: his book with Vijay Kelkar argues that the state’s failures cut across domains.

~ Amit Varma worried that any army is an anachronism in fast-moving times. Shah replied that large institutions everywhere change slowly, and that climbing past lower-middle income needs a culture of evidence, post-mortems and criticism. {#middleincome}

quote.text: War is too important to be left to the generals, and security is too important to be left to security people.

sections.label: The parting rant
sections.head: All of life at the tables
sections.caption: life as one long gamble
body: A stray memory closed the episode. Ajay Shah recalled an index, he thought from Bloomberg, built from listed companies that profit from each vice, gambling among them. {#vice}
Amit Varma, who was a professional poker player for five years, had a mini rant ready. {#poker} Poker is a game of skill, he said, and not pure gambling. But everything we do is a gamble.

Gambling, he said, is sussing up the probabilities and making a bet. A roulette wheel qualifies, but so does talking to a pretty woman in a bar, buying a house rumoured to be haunted because it is cheaper, or launching this show. {004-C14}
## Mistakes and freedoms

Shah, who has never gambled, agreed that exposing ourselves to risk is part of life. But lotteries, where you lose on average because the house always wins, and derivatives positions that burn through a balance sheet, were to him decision mistakes. {#lottery}
Varma answered that it is up to the individual to make those mistakes, and the state should not get involved. When Shah called lotteries a tax on the dumb, Varma asked who is to decide who is dumb.
~ He signed off the same way: anyone still watching had gambled on the show, and enjoyed it. {004-J07}

quote.text: Everything we do in our lives is gambling because after all, what is gambling?

side.boxText: Adam Smith warned, as Ajay Shah paraphrased him, that men of the same profession seldom get together without trying to rig the price. That is our mental model of cartels, Shah said, and OPEC put it to the test. {004-J08}

contQuote.text: If you’re saying Kashmir is an integral part of India, I strongly believe that that means that Kashmiri people are Indian people, you have to treat them like your own citizens.

stories.caption: the birth of the oil cartel
stories.kicker: Ajay Shah on how OPEC was born, and what it achieved
stories.head: Born in anger, beaten by time
body: Before 1973, Ajay Shah said, there had been a long and easy collaboration between the Arab oil producers, most notably Saudi Arabia, and the Western consumers of crude. It was live and let live, and OPEC had not yet found its feet.

Then came the 1973 war. The Arab countries had lost to Israel in 1967 and prepared for a rematch. They got their strategic surprise, but Israel picked itself up and won again, and the Arab street, Shah said, was left with humiliation, frustration and blinding hatred.
In that fit of anger, a group of oil-producing countries decided to raise the price of crude. They cut production by only 8 per cent, and the price went from about $1.5 a barrel to $11. {#cut8}
Later histories show that the producers themselves thought it reckless. Some powerful oil-consuming country, they feared, might simply land an army and grab the oil fields of the Persian Gulf.
Henry Kissinger, it is believed, wrote a pseudonymous magazine article setting out such an operation in detail, to turn the Gulf’s oil-producing regions into a global trust. {#kissinger}
No army came. “And suddenly the Arabs looked at each other saying, Wow, we got such a big increase in the oil price,” Shah said. The cartoon cartel was born.
~ Then he ran the numbers. Crude went from about $11 in 1974 to about $77 in 2023, and that, he said, is about 1.5 per cent a year in real terms over “the succeeding 53 years”. {004-S01}
stories.why: A price shock can look like proof of a cartel’s power, but it is often the short run talking. Given time, demand adjusts, victims route around extortion, and members with different needs cheat on one another. {004-C02}
stories.postscript: Fifty years later the story ran in reverse: after the 2022 war, India and China became a cartel of buyers. {004-S02}

stories.start: the first one which has stayed with me for a long time
stories.end: that you can figure shit out, you know, things often go wrong.
stories.caption: the father who calculated the ice
stories.kicker: Amit Varma on a father, a son and a frozen lake
stories.head: Within the margin of error
body: Krzysztof Kieślowski, the Polish filmmaker, was commissioned by Polish television to make ten short films on the Ten Commandments. {#tenfilms} Amit Varma calls the series, *Dekalog*, the pinnacle of cinematic storytelling.

The first film takes the commandment “Thou shalt not have any other god than me”. Its hero is a scientist, “very much like you”, Varma told Ajay Shah. The man’s young son is waiting for the lake to freeze so that he can go skating.

The father monitors the temperature every day, and the weather reports, and everything else. At last he concludes that today, within the margin of error, it is safe. The boy goes skating. The ice cracks, and he dies. {004-S05}
~ In the last shot the father stands by the lake. In the distance a homeless man has lit a fire to warm his hands.

quote.text: This film doesn’t have an anti-science message to me. Instead, it has an important humility message to me.

stories.start: a short film about love is basically about this kid in an apartment
stories.end: And that's such a great moment of show don't tell.
stories.caption: the boy on the bicycle
stories.kicker: Amit Varma on a scene he uses to teach writing
stories.head: Round and round in sheer joy
body: Two of the *Dekalog* films were made into longer films, and Amit Varma calls both masterpieces. {004-R17} In *A Short Film About Love*, a young man in an apartment complex has a crush on a woman across the way, and creepily spies on her through her window.
One day he decides to go up to her door, perhaps while delivering the milk or the papers, and ask her out. He rings the bell.

A stereotypical film, Varma said, would show the door opening, the question and her answer. Kieślowski cuts instead to a top-angle shot of the courtyard below, where the young man rides round and round on a cycle in sheer joy. {004-S06}
~ “And it just tells you everything,” Varma said. He uses the scene to teach his writing students.
stories.why: Show, don’t tell works even in cinema, Varma said. Kieślowski skips the obvious beats, the door, the question, the answer, and trusts one image of a young man on a bicycle to carry the emotion.

stories.start: when I go to Bangalore, I stay in Church Street
stories.end: which was on sale like everything else by Fred Kaplan called The Insurgents.
stories.caption: the best bookshop in the world
stories.kicker: Amit Varma on Church Street and the rival bookshop
stories.head: One copy too many
body: When Amit Varma goes to Bangalore, he stays on Church Street, home to the studio where he records, a Starbucks and Blossoms, his favourite bookshop in the world.

Once he recorded an episode of *The Seen and the Unseen* with Ram Guha. {#guha} When Varma said he was off to the best bookshop in the world, Guha, in Varma’s admittedly embellished retelling, called him a fool: Blossoms was not even the best on Church Street.

Guha’s pick was Bookworm. Varma visited both. “It turned out Bookworm actually had a copy of a shitty book I wrote a decade and a half ago,” he said. “So I immediately concluded Blossoms is better.” {004-S03}
~ Later, in Blossoms’ secondhand section, he found Fred Kaplan’s *The Insurgents* on sale. It began this episode’s rabbit hole. {004-R03}
stories.why: One chance find can open a whole field. For Varma, a book like Kaplan’s becomes an entry into a universe: he will then read 30 other books, going down rabbit hole after rabbit hole.
stories.postscript: If you go to Bali for a week, Varma said, he will go for a week to Blossoms. {004-J05}

quiz.q: What real yearly price rise did OPEC achieve from 1974 to 2023, by Shah’s count?
quiz.a: About 1.5 per cent a year, though the price rose roughly seven times.

quiz.q: How could the West cap the price of Russian oil sold to India and China?
quiz.a: Almost all the world’s shipping and shipping insurance is run from Western countries.

quiz.q: In Galula’s metaphor for guerrilla war, what can the fly and the lion not do?
quiz.a: The fly cannot deliver a knockout blow, and the lion cannot fly.

quiz.q: What ratio of military to political did one of Mao’s generals give counterinsurgency?
quiz.a: Twenty per cent military, eighty per cent political; India’s Kashmir approach was nearly all military.

quiz.q: In Mancur Olson’s model, why does a stationary bandit bother to build infrastructure?
quiz.a: He stays to tax the village year after year, since people are resources.

quiz.q: In the first film of Kieślowski’s *Dekalog*, what goes wrong for the scientist’s son?
quiz.a: His father calculates the lake ice is safe; it cracks and the boy dies.
